## What this suite is for

Where db-benchmark stresses group by and join in isolation, TPC-H stresses the optimizer. The wins here come from projection pushdown, predicate pushdown, join ordering and partition pruning rather than from kernel speed.

This is the suite that catches optimizer regressions, and it is the one that will hurt early, because DuckDB and Polars have had years on exactly these queries.

## Where the queries come from

The SQL is not ours. It is read out of DuckDB's `tpch` extension with `tpch_queries()`, which is the specification's own text, and DuckDB runs it unmodified. The pandas and Polars versions are ports, written once against the same text, and a port is where a benchmark goes wrong: a subquery turned into a join that drops rows, a filter applied after an aggregate instead of before it, a left join written as an inner one. Each of those produces a plausible table quickly, and a fast wrong answer is worse than no answer.

So every port is checked against `tpch_answers()`, the validation output the TPC publishes with the specification, cell by cell to a relative tolerance of a part in a million, including column names. All 66 implementations, three engines times twenty two queries, reproduce it at SF1. `pixi run validate-tpch` is what CI runs and a query that does not reproduce the published answer does not go in the results table.

Two things that check turned up, kept here because they will come back:

**Q18's column has no alias.** The select list says `sum(l_quantity)` and the published answer header abbreviates it to `sum`, so DuckDB running the specification's own text disagrees with the specification's own answer file. The select list is the better authority, both ports were renamed to match it, and the header check accepts a produced name that begins with the published one.

**Polars gives a decimal quotient the numerator's scale.** Q8's `mkt_share` came back as `0.03` rather than `0.0344358904066548`. Both operands are cast to Float64 in that one query.

## Which engines run it

All four run all 22, at SF1 and at SF10. firepanda's row count and exact answer digest match pandas' and DuckDB's on every query at both sizes. Polars' digest differs on a handful of the revenue sums, four at SF1 and three at SF10, which is float summation order in the last bits and not a wrong answer, and the harness' tolerance comparison passes them.

One thing about firepanda's load path is worth stating because it is visible in the memory column. firepanda can open a Parquet file, but it does so by handing it to DuckDB, so a firepanda run holds DuckDB's copy of the table and its own at the same time. That is most of why it is the only engine in the table that uses more memory than pandas, and it is why the `--io scan` tables are not published yet: timing firepanda on a Parquet reader that is DuckDB's reader would not be measuring firepanda.

At SF10 that load path stops being a footnote. firepanda peaked at 31.57 GB on a machine with 31 GB of RAM, so the lineitem heavy queries there were running against a machine that had started paging, while Polars peaked at 21.05 GB and stayed inside memory. The SF10 numbers are reported as measured and the per query times for firepanda should be read as an upper bound rather than as what the engine does with room to work in.

pandas gets one concession that is worth stating plainly. Arrow-backed pandas cannot do the decimal arithmetic Q1 needs, because the intermediate wants precision 61 and Arrow's limit is 38, and there is no way to ask for a narrower one. Decimal columns are cast to double at load. Double arithmetic is faster than exact decimal arithmetic, so the bias runs in pandas' favour.

## Two queries get called out by name

**Q18** is the MojoFrame comparison. MojoFrame supports all 22 queries and reports up to 4.60x over dataframe libraries in other languages, and its authors published where it falls behind, which is high-cardinality aggregation, diagnosed as Mojo's dictionary. firepanda claims to have fixed that by writing its own hash table.

Q18 is now the query that answers the claim, and the answer is yes. It is firepanda's widest margin in the suite at both sizes: 3.44x Polars and 2.67x DuckDB at SF1, and 4.02x Polars and 2.17x DuckDB at SF10. It is also the only query that clears 2x against all three rivals at SF10. That is a group by on one and a half million order keys followed by a semi join against a grouped subquery, which is the high cardinality aggregation case named above, so the hash table is doing what it was written to do.

**Q13** is UDF-heavy, and it is where the language argument should show up as a number. The entire premise of writing this library in Mojo is that the user's own function compiles into the pipeline instead of being called through an interpreter. If that is worth anything, Q13 is one of the places it becomes visible in a standard suite rather than in one we designed ourselves.

## Data

`dbgen` from DuckDB's `tpch` extension, written out as Parquet. SF1 is 8 tables, 392 MB uncompressed, with 6,001,215 line items, and takes about eleven seconds to generate. SF10 is ten times that. Generated once and cached under `data/tpch/<size>/`, not regenerated per run.

Parquet rather than CSV because these queries are about the optimizer, and Parquet is what lets projection pushdown and row-group skipping show up at all. That only applies in `--io scan`; the default `memory` mode hands every engine the same Arrow table so nobody is timed on their Parquet reader.

## Reported

Per-query timing with the full spread, peak resident set, user and system CPU, and page faults. The number of columns decoded and row groups read is still to come for firepanda and waits on its own Parquet reader, since the counters would otherwise be DuckDB's. Those counters are how a pushdown regression is distinguished from a machine having a bad day.

## Q11's fraction, which was the open question before SF10

Q11 filters on a fraction of total value, and a strict reading of the specification scales that fraction by the scale factor. The ports hardcode 0.0001, and this needed settling before SF10 went into the tables.

It is settled, and the answer is that DuckDB's query text hardcodes it too. `tpch_queries()` is scale independent and the subquery reads `sum(ps_supplycost * ps_availqty) * 0.0001000000` whatever size the data is. So all four engines compute the same filter at SF10 and their answers agree exactly, which is what the comparison needs. It is worth being clear that this makes SF10's Q11 DuckDB's Q11 rather than the specification's: a reading that scaled the fraction would keep roughly the same number of parts as SF1 where this one keeps ten times as many.

There is no way to check SF10 against the published output regardless. `tpch_answers()` carries validation output for scale factors 0.01, 0.1 and 1.0 and nothing above that, so `pixi run validate-tpch` runs at SF1 and the SF10 claim is cross engine agreement rather than agreement with the TPC.
